analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal regulator solely dedicated to banning predatory and deceptive consumer credit practices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced as the 2008 financial crisis hit, never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee with zero cosponsors and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new, independent Consumer Credit Safety Commission with one job: policing consumer credit products the way other agencies police product safety. It would have had power to ban abusive, deceptive, predatory, or anticompetitive lending and fee practices, set clear disclosure requirements, run a consumer complaint hotline, and impose civil and criminal penalties on violators, including individual executives. The bill was introduced October 3, 2008, weeks after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, and went no further than a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary borrowers: credit card holders hit with late, over-limit, and cash-advance fees; people with weak credit facing predatory loan products; small businesses defined as consumers under the bill; and anyone who wanted a single regulator focused on whether credit products are safe rather than whether lenders are sound. The bill also directed the Commission to consider the special needs of elderly and disabled consumers and barred preemption of stronger state consumer protection laws.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a five-member independent commission empowered to ban abusive, fraudulent, unfair, deceptive, predatory, and anticompetitive consumer credit practices and product features [S2][S3].

The bill defines 'consumer credit' broadly to cover not just interest but late fees, over-limit fees, cash advance fees, and payment-system charges like interchange and merchant discount fees, bringing the whole cost of borrowing under one regulator's watch [S3].
Requires a consumer hotline for complaints, a best-practices guide for lenders, ongoing investigations of industry practices, and public reports naming companies and enforcement actions [S2][S3].

Imposes criminal penalties of up to $500,000 and one year in prison on executives who knowingly and willfully violate bans after notice, and lets the Commission set civil penalties per violating transaction [S3].
Preserves stronger state consumer protection laws from preemption and directs the Commission to account for the special needs of elderly and disabled consumers when writing rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer credit providers: banks, credit card issuers, consumer lenders, and payment companies would face a new regulator with rulemaking power over their products, fees, and marketing, plus civil penalties per transaction and potential criminal liability for executives. Taxpayers would fund the Commission through appropriations, though the bill also lets it retain collected fines and buy credit products at cost for study.

drawbacks.text: A single Commission regulating every consumer credit product in the country could restrict access to credit for higher-risk borrowers, since banning costly products can leave some consumers with fewer borrowing options; the bill itself requires the Commission to weigh each rule's effect on the cost and availability of credit [S3].

The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in appropriations with no cost estimate, and creates an entirely new agency with offices, staff paid at SEC levels, hotline operations, and enforcement staff [S3].

The Commission's authority overlaps ten existing financial regulators, from the Federal Reserve to the FTC, raising coordination problems even though the bill names them as cooperating enforcement agencies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's consumer protections were broad and structural: it targeted the fee and payment-system charges that make credit expensive, not just headline interest rates, and it kept states free to go further. The main honest trade-off is that policing dangerous credit products can reduce credit availability for some borrowers, and a new agency carries real cost. The design anticipated both problems with mandatory cost-benefit findings for every rule and cooperative enforcement with existing agencies, but it was never tested: it died in committee without even a single cosponsor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on October 3, 2008, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and nothing else ever happened to it; the committee never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Delahunt introduced the bill on October 3, 2008, about two weeks after Lehman Brothers' collapse deepened the financial crisis [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, whose action history shows no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind [S5].
The bill's findings echoed the crisis moment, stating that dispersed regulation had allowed excessively costly or predatory consumer credit products to flourish [S3].

The idea it contained — a standalone regulator whose sole focus is consumer credit safety — resurfaced two years later in a much-debated form as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau in the Dodd-Frank Act [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer credit providers, including credit card issuers and other lenders, avoided a new regulator with power over their fees and products, because the bill never advanced beyond referral. Consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer lenders who avoided a new regulator

for.name: Rep. William Delahunt
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on October 3, 2008

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 3, 2008 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred, so no party split is recorded; the single sponsor was a Democrat and the committee that let the bill sit was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: A new commission could ban their fee-heavy and predatory products and impose civil penalties per transaction plus criminal exposure for executives. Its interest in stopping the bill ran against consumers' interest in cheaper, safer credit.

The bill's definition of consumer credit explicitly sweeps in interchange, merchant discount, and debit card fees, putting payment-system charges under the new regulator's rulemaking power. Networks would lose pricing freedom over fees consumers ultimately bear.

The bill's stated purpose includes giving 'sellers of consumer credit more regulatory certainty' and directing the Commission to help providers develop safety standards and compliance guides, so compliant lenders would gain a stable rulebook. That certainty came bundled with a new enforcement regime.
